title: NTA UGC NET English Full Mock Test #16
subtitle: 100 Questions · 200 Marks · Post-2018 NTA Pattern · Zero Answer Bias (25 A/B/C/D) · Reading Comprehension (Q91-100)

items.title: Mock #16 · Q1
items.stem:
Match the column:
(A) “So much depends upon a red wheel barrow”
(B) “Your mind and you are our Sargasso Sea”
(C) “Spring is like a perhaps hand (which comes carefully out of nowhere) arranging a window”
(D) “I caught the cold flash of the blue unappearable sky”
(I) Ezra Pound
(II) Stanley Kunitz
(III) William Carlos Williams
(IV) E. E. Cummings
items.explanation: William Carlos Williams wrote the Imagist poem 'The Red Wheelbarrow' containing 'So much depends upon a red wheel barrow' (A-III); Ezra Pound penned 'Portrait d'une Femme' opening with 'Your mind and you are our Sargasso Sea' (B-I); E. E. Cummings wrote 'Spring is like a perhaps hand' (C-IV); and Stanley Kunitz wrote 'I caught the cold flash of the blue unappearable sky' (D-II).

items.title: Mock #16 · Q2
items.stem:
One of the most quoted statements on poetry by John Keats is reproduced with blanks
below. Complete the statement with correct words.
“If Poetry __________ as naturally as the leaves to a tree, it __________ at all”.
options: does not come; had better not come
come not; had better not come
items.explanation: In a letter to his publisher John Taylor on 27 February 1818, John Keats articulated his 'axioms' of poetics, including: 'That if Poetry come not as naturally as the Leaves to a tree it had better not come at all.'

items.title: Mock #16 · Q3
items.stem:
Two of the following words were borrowed from French after the Norman Conquest.
(a)
mutton
(b)
pork
(c)
sheep
(d)
swine
The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: Following the Norman Conquest of 1066, English borrowed French culinary words for cooked meats served to the Norman nobility—such as 'mutton' (from Old French moton) and 'pork' (from Old French porc)—while retaining native Old English words ('sheep' and 'swine') for the living farm animals tended by Anglo-Saxon peasants.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q4
items.stem: Erich Auerbach's Mimesis (1946) ends with a chapter on:
options: Wyndham Lewis's The Apes of God
items.explanation: Erich Auerbach's Mimesis: The Representation of Reality in Western Literature (1946) concludes with Chapter 20, 'The Brown Stocking,' which analyzes stream-of-consciousness narration in Virginia Woolf's To the Lighthouse (1927).

items.title: Mock #16 · Q5
items.stem:
Find the chronological order of publication of the given works:
A. Mythologies
B. Of Grammatology
C. Culture and Society
D. Blindness and Insight
E. The Location of Culture

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The correct chronological order of first publication is: Roland Barthes's Mythologies (1957, A), Raymond Williams's Culture and Society (1958, C), Jacques Derrida's Of Grammatology (1967, B), Paul de Man's Blindness and Insight (1971, D), and Homi K. Bhabha's The Location of Culture (1994, E).

items.title: Mock #16 · Q6
items.stem: Samuel Johnson wrote London in imitation of __________.
items.explanation: Samuel Johnson published London (1738) as a verse satire composed in imitation of Juvenal's Third Satire (depicting the corruption, crime, and poverty of metropolitan city life).

items.title: Mock #16 · Q7
items.stem:
Assertion (A) : "Standard English" is a misleading term.
Reason (R) : Because linguistic communities do not actually possess a genuine standard variety.
In the context of the two statements, which one of the following is correct ?
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
items.explanation: Per the official UGC key, both (A) and (R) are treated as true sociolinguistic observations regarding the idealized and socially constructed nature of 'Standard English', with option (B) selected.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q8
items.stem:
Name the theorist who divided poets
into
"strong"
and
"weak"
and
popularized
the
practice
of
misreading
items.explanation: In The Anxiety of Influence (1973) and A Map of Misreading (1975), American critic Harold Bloom argued that 'strong' poets overcome the stifling influence of their great predecessors through creative 'misreading' (misprision), whereas 'weak' poets merely imitate them.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q9
items.stem:
Who among the following poets have lived in Australia?
A. Judith Wright
B. Yusef Komunyakaa
C. Kath Walker
D. Thomas Kinsella
E. T. S. Eliot
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Judith Wright (A) and Aboriginal poet Kath Walker / Oodgeroo Noonuccal (C) were native Australian poets, and African American Pulitzer Prize-winning poet Yusef Komunyakaa (B) lived in Australia for over a decade beginning in the mid-1980s.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q10
items.stem: Which of the following is the accurate description of 'dramatic irony'?
options: An audience knows or expects something to happen but the events on stage turn out to be different
A character's knowledge or expectation is contradicted by what the audience knows, or by the outcome of events
Ironic events and expectations of actual actions and results converge in drama and the audience feels rewarded
A dramatist's irony reinforces his actors' performance, thereby fulfilling audience expectations
items.explanation: In dramatic irony the audience knows more than a character does, so the character's words or hopes are contradicted.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q11
items.stem:
Match the List-I with List-II
List I (Books/Collection of Poems):
A. The Idylls of the King
B. Dramatic Lyrics
C. Sonnets from the Portuguese
D. Poems and Ballads

List II (Poet):
I. Elizabeth Barrett Browning
II. A.C. Swinburne
III. Alfred Tennyson
IV. Robert Browning

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The Victorian poetry collections match their poets as follows: Idylls of the King (1859–85) by Alfred, Lord Tennyson (A-III), Dramatic Lyrics (1842) by Robert Browning (B-IV), Sonnets from the Portuguese (1850) by Elizabeth Barrett Browning (C-I), and Poems and Ballads (1866) by Algernon Charles Swinburne (D-II).

items.title: Mock #16 · Q12
items.stem: The plays which are based on the Biblical stories are known as
items.explanation: Medieval Mystery plays dramatized biblical narratives from the Creation to the Last Judgment and were performed by trade guilds (craft 'mysteries'). Miracle plays depicted the lives and miracles of saints, while Morality plays used allegorical characters to teach moral lessons.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q13
items.stem:
Identify the incorrect statement below :

(a)
BASIC
was
an
experiment
initiated by C. K. Ogden and
I. A. Richards from 1926 to
about 1940.

(b)
Expanded, BASIC read : Broadly
Ascertained
Scientific
International Course.

(c)
BASIC English was an attempt
to reduce the number of essential
words to 850.

(d)
While
keeping
to
normal
constructions, BASIC failed as
an

because
its

were

items.explanation: Statements (b) and (d) are incorrect: the acronym BASIC in C. K. Ogden and I. A. Richards's Basic English project stood for 'British American Scientific International Commercial' (not 'Broadly Ascertained Scientific International Course'), and its texts were intentionally written in a simple 850-word vocabulary rather than complicated technical jargon.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q14
items.stem:
Who among the following Greek Philosophers has a bearing on the composition of
Shelley's "Adonais" ?
items.explanation: P. B. Shelley's pastoral elegy Adonais (1821), written on the death of John Keats, is deeply shaped by Plato's philosophy and opens with an epigraph in Greek taken from an epigram on Aster attributed to Plato.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q15
items.stem:
Arrange the following poems by W. B. Yeats in the chronological order of publication.
 A. "The Wild Swans at Coole"
 B. "The Second Coming"
 C. "Among School Children"
 D. "Adam's Curse"
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: The chronological order of these poems by W.B. Yeats is 'Adam's Curse' (1902/1903, D), 'The Wild Swans at Coole' (1917, A), 'The Second Coming' (1920, B), and 'Among School Children' (1927, C).

items.title: Mock #16 · Q16
items.stem: In Herman Melville’s well-known story “Bartleby the Scrivener”, what does the word “scrivener” mean?
options: Pasting clerks in a Dead Letter Office
Articled clerks in an accountant’s office
Clerks who serve as personal assistants to judges.
Clerks who copy legal documents by hand.
items.explanation: In Herman Melville's 1853 story "Bartleby, the Scrivener: A Story of Wall-Street", a scrivener was a professional legal clerk employed to hand-copy legal documents, contracts, and court records before the development of commercial typewriters.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q17
items.stem:
Assertion (A) : Gustave Flaubert's Madame Bovary Stratified a distinct space for the novel in the mid-nineteenth century because of its formal perfection and lack of rhetorical embellishment.
Reason (R) : Flaubert hated the bourgeoisie and believed that the artist should stand outside the utilitarian values of middle-class society.
Codes :
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
items.explanation: Flaubert's contempt for bourgeois clichés and utilitarian sentimentality (R) directly motivated his aesthetic doctrine of impersonal objectivity and stylistic precision (le mot juste) in Madame Bovary (1856) (A).

items.title: Mock #16 · Q18
items.stem: Which of the following is considered to be the first Indian novel in English?
options: K.K. Sinha’s The Star of Sikri
items.explanation: Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's Rajamohan's Wife, published serially in 1864 in the periodical Indian Field, is historically recognized as the first published Indian novel in English.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q19
items.stem:
Bertolt Brecht's Epic Theatre

(a)
turns the spectator into an
observer

(b)
wears
down
the
spectator's
capacity for action

(c)
relies on argument

(d)
presents man as a process
options: (a) and (d) are correct; (b) and (c) are incorrect
(b) and (d) are correct; (a) and (c) are incorrect
items.explanation: In his 1930 notes to the opera Rise and Fall of the City of Mahagonny, Bertolt Brecht explained that Epic Theatre turns the spectator into a critical observer (a), relies on rational argument (c), and presents human beings as alterable and 'as a process' (d), while arousing—rather than wearing down (b)—the spectator's capacity for action.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q20
items.stem: Michel Foucault's earlier "archaeological" study is found in
items.explanation: Michel Foucault introduced the concept of the 'medical gaze' (regard médical) in his 1963 book The Birth of the Clinic: An Archaeology of Medical Perception (Naissance de la clinique), tracing how late-eighteenth-century clinical medicine reorganized knowledge around anatomical observation of the patient's body.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q21
items.meta: Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem:
Match the column:
A. Surprised by Sin: the Reader in “Paradise :Lost”
B. Five Readers Reading
C. The Reader, the Text, the Poem
D. With Respect to Readers
I. Louise Rosenblatt
II. Stanley Fish
III. Walter J Slatoff
IV. Norman Holland
items.explanation: These landmark reader-response critical texts match their authors: Stanley Fish wrote *Surprised by Sin: The Reader in Paradise Lost* (A-II, 1967), Norman Holland authored *Five Readers Reading* (B-IV, 1975), Louise Rosenblatt published *The Reader, the Text, the Poem* (C-I, 1978), and Walter J. Slatoff wrote *With Respect to Readers* (D-III, 1970).

items.title: Mock #16 · Q22
items.stem: "To see him act is like reading Shakespeare by flashes of lighting." About which Shakespearean actor Coleridge wrote the above line?
items.explanation: Coleridge said this of Edmund Kean, whose acting was brilliant in sudden flashes.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q23
items.stem:
The lives of which of the following writers have been the subject matter of novels by Anthony
Burgess?

A. Milton

B. Marlowe

C. Shelley

D. Keats

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: British novelist Anthony Burgess wrote biographical novels about several English writers, including Christopher Marlowe in A Dead Man in Deptford (1993), John Keats in ABBA ABBA (1977, depicting Keats's final months in Rome), and William Shakespeare in Nothing Like the Sun (1964).

items.title: Mock #16 · Q24
items.stem: What does 'Harlem Renaissance' refer to?
options: A scientific and rational ethos, including freedom from superstition, in 18th century Europe
The flourishing of African American literature in the 1920s and 1930s
A church system, overseen by a governing hierarchy of four courts, championed by the English Puritans
The revelation of Christ to the Gentiles in the persons of the Magi
items.explanation: The Harlem Renaissance was the cultural and literary flowering of African American writers and artists in the 1920s and 1930s.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q25
items.stem:
Arrange the following poets in accordance with their years of birth.
A. Rudyard Kipling
B. Robert Browning
C. John Masefield
D. A. E. Housman
E. John Donne
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The birth years of the five poets are: John Donne (1572, E), Robert Browning (1812, B), A.E. Housman (1859, D), Rudyard Kipling (1865, A), and John Masefield (1878, C), matching the option E, B, A, D, C.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q26
items.stem:
What work begins thus : "It befell in the days of Uther Pendragon, when he was king of all
England, and so reigned, that there was a mighty duke in Cornwall that held war against
him long time" ?
options: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
items.explanation: Sir Thomas Malory's prose romance Le Morte d'Arthur (printed by William Caxton in 1485) begins Book I, Chapter 1 with this famous sentence recounting King Uther Pendragon's war against the Duke of Tintagel in Cornwall and his passion for Igraine.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q27
items.stem:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: All research being original and uninspired, it is rare for a researcher to begin a project by deriving ideas
from predecessors.
Statement II: Studying and documenting past work on a research topic stifles the continual expansion of human
knowledge.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
items.explanation: Both statements are incorrect: scholarly research always builds upon a thorough literature review of prior scholarship, and documenting earlier work is essential to advancing rather than stifling human knowledge.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q28
items.stem: Who composed the poem "The Phoenix and the Turtle"?
items.explanation: 'The Phoenix and the Turtle' is an enigmatic allegorical poem by William Shakespeare, first published in 1601 in Robert Chester's collection Love's Martyr. It commemorates the mystical spiritual union and mutual demise of the mythical phoenix and the devoted turtle-dove.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q29
items.stem:
Which of the following two books have their roots in Foucauldian thoughts on sexuality?
A. Metahistory
B. Gender Trouble: Feminism and the Subversion of Identity
C. The Role of the Reader
D. Epistemology of the Closet
E. Sexual Politics
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Judith Butler's Gender Trouble: Feminism and the Subversion of Identity (1990) (B) and Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick's Epistemology of the Closet (1990) (D) are foundational queer-theory texts directly rooted in Michel Foucault's The History of Sexuality (1976).

items.title: Mock #16 · Q30
items.stem:
The translation of Geeta into English in 1784 called Bhagvit - Geeta marked, in William Jones's
opinion, an "event that made it possible for the first time to have a reliable impression of
Indian Literature".  Who was the translator ?
items.explanation: Orientalist scholar Sir Charles Wilkins, a founding member of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, completed the first direct Sanskrit-to-English translation of the Bhagavad Gita (published in London in 1785 as The Bhagvat-Geeta, or Dialogues of Kreeshna and Arjoon) with a preface by Warren Hastings.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q31
items.stem:
Match the column:
(Term)
A. et sq.
B. idem
C. loc. cit.
D. passim
(Meaning)
I. the same
II. in the place cited
III. everywhere
IV. and the following
items.explanation: These Latin citation abbreviations used in academic research translate as: *et sq.* (*et sequentes*) means 'and the following' (A-IV), *idem* means 'the same' (B-I), *loc. cit.* (*loco citato*) means 'in the place cited' (C-II), and *passim* means 'everywhere' or throughout the work (D-III).

items.title: Mock #16 · Q32
items.stem: Which among the following is an incomplete poem by P. B. Shelley?
items.explanation: 'The Triumph of Life' (composed in terza rima in the spring and summer of 1822 and published posthumously by Mary Shelley in Posthumous Poems, 1824) was left incomplete when Percy Bysshe Shelley drowned in the Gulf of Spezia on 8 July 1822.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q33
items.stem:
Which statement(s) below on the Spenserian Stanza is/are accurate ?
I. a quatrain, unrhymed, but alliterative
II. a stanza of four lines in iambic pentameter
III. an eight-line stanza in iambic pentameter followed by a ninth in six iambic feet
IV. an eight-line stanza with six iambic feet followed by a ninth in iambic pentameter
items.explanation: Invented by Edmund Spenser for The Faerie Queene (1590–1596), the Spenserian stanza consists of eight lines in iambic pentameter followed by a ninth alexandrine line in iambic hexameter (six iambic feet), rhyming ababbcbcc (III).

items.title: Mock #16 · Q34
items.stem:
'Aucitya' refers to :

I.
Decorum

II.
Propriety

III.
Proportion

IV.
Accuracy
items.explanation: Systematized by the eleventh-century Sanskrit theorist Kshemendra in his Aucityavicaracarca, the school of Aucitya in Indian poetics specifically denotes 'propriety' or appropriateness of poetic expression, which Kshemendra called the very soul of rasa-filled poetry.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q35
items.stem: Identify the correct chronological sequence of the following early English texts
options: Troilus and Criseyde - The Owl and The Nightingale - Utopia - Morte d'Arthur
Troilus and Criseyde - Utopia - Morte d'Arthur - The Owl and the Nightingale
The Owl and the Nightingale - Morte d'Arthur - Troilus and Criseyde - Uttopia
The Owl and the Nightingale - Troilus and Criseyde - Morte d'Arthur - Utopia
items.explanation: The correct chronological sequence of these early texts is the Middle English debate poem The Owl and the Nightingale (c. 1200), Geoffrey Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde (c. 1385), Sir Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur (completed c. 1470, printed 1485), and Sir Thomas More's Utopia (1516).

items.title: Mock #16 · Q36
items.stem: Which among the following does not relate to Universal Grammar?
options: Universal grammar is a theoretical concept proposed by Edward Sapir
It suggests that all languages possess the same set of categories and relations
It is based on the idea that certain aspects of syntactic structure are universal
Itis based on the postulate that the human brain contains an innate mental grammar
items.explanation: Universal Grammar is the foundational linguistic theory formulated by Noam Chomsky, not Edward Sapir (who is known for the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis of linguistic relativity). Chomsky proposed that humans are born with an innate language faculty comprising structural principles common to all human languages.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q37
items.stem:
Given below are two statements, one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R) :
Assertion (A) : The literature of the Jacobean Age is dominated by the mood of melodrama and sensationalism.
Reason (R) : The literature of the Jacobean Age was steeped in the spirit of decadence.
In the context of the two statements, which one of the following is correct ?
Codes :
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
items.explanation: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are valid: the mid-nineteenth century in Britain was characterized by profound intellectual debate between science and orthodox religious faith (spurred by geology and Darwinian evolutionary theory), which directly animated the anxieties and religious questionings in the poetry of Tennyson, Arnold, and Clough.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q38
items.stem: Identify the two Indian texts translated by the Orientalist William Jones I. Abhignanamshakuntalam II. Katha Sarita Sagar III. Mahabharatha IV. Manusmriti The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: Sir William Jones translated Kalidasa's Sanskrit play Abhijnanasakuntalam (as Sacontalá in 1789, statement I) and the ancient Hindu code Manusmriti (as Institutes of Hindu Law in 1794, statement IV). The Katha Sarit Sagara was translated by C.H. Tawney, and the Mahabharata by K.M. Ganguli.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q39
items.stem:
Which of the following works have been authored by Thomas De Quincey?
A. Confessions of An English Opium Eater
B. The French Revolution
C. Hudibras
D. Autobiography
E. Suspiria De Profoundis
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Romantic essayist Thomas De Quincey authored Confessions of an English Opium-Eater (1821, A), Autobiographic Sketches (1853, D), and its sequel Suspiria de Profundis (1845, E). The French Revolution is by Thomas Carlyle and Hudibras is by Samuel Butler.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q40
items.stem:
Who among the following critics appropriates the following statement by Karl Marx?
"They cannot represent themselves : they must be represented".
items.explanation: Postcolonial feminist theorist Chandra Talpade Mohanty (alongside Edward Said in Orientalism and Spivak in 'Can the Subaltern Speak?') appropriates Karl Marx's line from The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte to critique Western feminism's homogenizing representation of Third World women.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q41
items.stem:
Match List - I with List - II. (List - I: Authors, List - II: Texts)
List - I | List - II
(A) Christopher Marlowe | (I) The Winter's Tale
(B) William Shakespeare | (II) The Jew of Malta
(C) Thomas Kyd | (III) Every Man in his Humour
(D) Ben Jonson | (IV) Spanish Tragedy
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The Renaissance dramatists match their plays as follows: Christopher Marlowe wrote The Jew of Malta (A-II), William Shakespeare wrote The Winter's Tale (B-I), Thomas Kyd wrote The Spanish Tragedy (C-IV), and Ben Jonson wrote Every Man in His Humour (D-III).

items.title: Mock #16 · Q42
items.stem:
Who among the following is not an
American modernist poet ?
items.explanation: William Ellery Channing the Younger (1818–1901) was a nineteenth-century American Transcendentalist poet and close friend of Henry David Thoreau, whereas William Carlos Williams, Ezra Pound, and Marianne Moore were leading twentieth-century American Modernist poets.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q43
items.stem:
Some of the following poets adorned the Oxford Professor of Poetry Chair:
A. James Fenton
B. Margaret Atwood
C. Seamus Heaney
D. Anne Sexton
E. Paul Muldoon
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Seamus Heaney (1989–1994, C), James Fenton (1994–1999, A), and Paul Muldoon (1999–2004, E) all held the prestigious post of Oxford Professor of Poetry, whereas Canadian writer Margaret Atwood and American confessional poet Anne Sexton never held the chair.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q44
items.stem: What is the full-form of APA?
items.explanation: APA stands for the American Psychological Association, the prominent US scientific organization whose official style guide is standardly used for citations across the social sciences and education.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q45
items.stem:
Arrange the following sentences in the order in which they appear in Emerson’s
“Self-Reliance” :
(a)
To be great is to be misunderstood.
(b)
Pythagoras was misunderstood, and Socrates, and Jesus, and Luther, and Copernicus,
and Galileo, and Newton, and every pure and wise spirit that ever took flesh.
(c)
If it so bad then to be misunderstood!
(d)
It is a right fool’s word.
(e)
Misunderstood!
items.explanation: In Ralph Waldo Emerson's essay 'Self-Reliance' (1841), the memorable passage reads: 'Misunderstood! (e) It is a right fool’s word. (d) Is it so bad then to be misunderstood? (c) Pythagoras was misunderstood, and Socrates... (b) To be great is to be misunderstood. (a)'

items.title: Mock #16 · Q46
items.stem: Identify the period during which the Puritans under the rule of Oliver Cromwell and his Commonwealth shut down all English theatres on religious and moral grounds :
items.explanation: Although the Long Parliament first ordered the closure of theatres in 1642 at the outbreak of the Civil War, the Interregnum period specifically under Oliver Cromwell and the Puritan Commonwealth lasted from the execution of Charles I in 1649 until the Restoration in 1660 (1649–1660).

items.title: Mock #16 · Q47
items.stem:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R
Assertion A: The defining event of the first part of the twenty-first century was the attack on American targets, including the Twin Towers in New York, on 11 September 2001.
Reason R: A novel by Christopher Brookmyre published two days before the attacks happened, A Big Boy Did It and Ran Away, was, and still is, astonishingly prescient both about the violence and about some of its roots and resonances.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is not correct
A is not correct but R is correct
items.explanation: Both statements are true observations from Carter and McRae's The Routledge History of Literature in English regarding the September 11, 2001 attacks and Scottish novelist Christopher Brookmyre's prescient novel A Big Boy Did It and Ran Away (2001), though R is not the cause of A.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q48
items.stem: Shel is a character in Virginia Woolf’s novel ……………
items.explanation: Marmaduke Bonthrop Shelmerdine, known affectionately as Shel, is the romantic seaman whom the protagonist meets on the moors and marries in Virginia Woolf's novel Orlando (1928).

items.title: Mock #16 · Q49
items.stem:
Which two of the following are part of Virginia Woolf’s collection of autobiographical essays?
(A) “A Will to Word It”
(B) “A Sketch of the Past”
(C) “A Faint Hue of the Past”
(D) “Am I a Snob”
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: Moments of Being includes 'A Sketch of the Past' and 'Am I a Snob?'. The other two titles are invented.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q50
items.stem:
"That glory never shall his wrath or
might extort from me." (Paradise
Lost, Book I)

What 'glory' is being referred to by
Satan ?
options: The courage never to submit or yield
items.explanation: In Book I of John Milton's Paradise Lost (1667), Satan addresses Beelzebub after their fall into Hell, boasting that God's wrath can never extort from him the glory of his unconquerable will and "courage never to submit or yield."

items.title: Mock #16 · Q51
items.stem:
Match the column:
A. Night of the Scorpion
B. Unfinished poem
C. The looking glass
D. To a friend far away
I. Kamala Das
II. A.K. Ramanujan
III. Eunice de Souza
IV. Nissim Ezekiel

items.title: Mock #16 · Q95
items.stem:

Lying is an accursed vice. It is only our words which bind us together and make us human. If we realized the horror and weight of lying, we would see that it is more worthy of the stake than other crimes. I find that people normally waste time quite inappropriately punishing children for innocent misdemeanours, tormenting them for thoughtless actions which lead nowhere and leave no trace. It seems to me that the only faults which we should vigorously attack as soon as they arise and start to develop are lying and, a little below that, stubbornness. Those faults grow up with the children. Once let the tongue acquire the habit of lying and it is astonishing how impossible it is to make it give it up. That is why some otherwise decent men are abject slaves to it. One of my tailors is a good enough fellow, but I have never heard him once speak the truth, not even when it would help him, if he did so.

options: It promotes togetherness among diverse people
It reduces the affinity among people
It does not affect at all as it is merely words.
items.explanation: In this passage from Michel de Montaigne's essay 'Of Liars', the author states that 'It is only our words which bind us together and make us human.' Consequently, lying corrupts the bond of mutual trust and reduces the affinity among people.

items.explanation: The passage states that people waste time punishing children for 'innocent misdemeanours, tormenting them for thoughtless actions which lead nowhere and leave no trace'—meaning such actions are inconsequential and soon forgotten.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q97
items.meta: Unit IV / Unit VIII: Prose & Criticism
items.stem:
Read the following passage and answer the questions :

Lying is an accursed vice. It is only our words which bind us together and make us human. If we realized the horror and weight of lying, we would see that it is more worthy of the stake than other crimes. I find that people normally waste time quite inappropriately punishing children for innocent misdemeanours, tormenting them for thoughtless actions which lead nowhere and leave no trace. It seems to me that the only faults which we should vigorously attack as soon as they arise and start to develop are lying and, a little below that, stubbornness. Those faults grow up with the children. Once let the tongue acquire the habit of lying and it is astonishing how impossible it is to make it give it up. That is why some otherwise decent men are abject slaves to it. One of my tailors is a good enough fellow, but I have never heard him once speak the truth, not even when it would help him, if he did so.

'Lying' is a fault that should be punished only
options: When the first lie is uttered
When it begins to turn into a habit
items.explanation: In this comprehension passage from Michel de Montaigne's essay 'Of Liars', the author states that instead of punishing children for harmless, thoughtless misdemeanours, we should punish lying as soon as it arises and 'begins to turn into a habit' that enslaves the tongue.

items.title: Mock #16 · Q99
items.meta: Unit IV / Unit VIII: Prose & Criticism
items.stem:
Read the following passage from Antigone and answer the question :

Creon : And yet wert bold enough to break the law.
Antigone : Yea, for these laws were not ordained by Zeus,
And she who sits enthroned with gods below,
Justice, enacted not these human laws.
Nor did I deem that thou, a mortal man,
Could'st by a breath annul and override
The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven.

The three kinds of laws implicit in Antigone's response are :
options: Of Gods, of Justice, of Man
Of Gods, of Zeus, of Justice
Of Man, of Heaven, of Zeus
items.explanation: In this speech from Sophocles' Antigone, Antigone contrasts three domains of law: the divine laws of the Gods (Zeus and the immutable unwritten laws of Heaven), the chthonic law of Justice ('she who sits enthroned with gods below'), and the mortal decrees of Man (Creon's 'human laws').

Read the following passage and answer the question :

It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief, it was the epoch of incredulity, it was the season of Light, it was the season of Darkness, it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair, we had everything before us, we had nothing before us, we were all going direct to Heaven, we were all going direct the other way — in short, the period was so far like the present period, that some of its noisiest authorities insisted on its being received, for good or for evil, in the superlative degree of comparison only.

The Age described in the above passage is best described as the Age of
items.explanation: This famous opening paragraph of Charles Dickens's A Tale of Two Cities (1859) characterizes the era of the French Revolution through a series of antithetical, polar-opposite pairs (best/worst, wisdom/foolishness, belief/incredulity, Light/Darkness, hope/despair), portraying it as an 'Age of Contraries'.
